# CLEANING
```{r}
to_min <- function(x) {
  map_dbl(strsplit(as.character(x), ":"),
          ~ as.numeric(.x[1]) + as.numeric(.x[2]) / 60)
}

nhl <- hockey_raw %>%
  group_by(Rk) %>% slice(1) %>% ungroup() %>%      # one row per player
  mutate(
    ATOI_min = to_min(ATOI),
    Pos3     = case_when(Pos == "D" ~ "D", Pos == "C" ~ "C", TRUE ~ "Wing"),
    Group2   = ifelse(Pos == "D", "Defense", "Forward"),
    AgeGroup = cut(Age, c(0, 22, 26, 30, Inf),
                   labels = c("<=22", "23-26", "27-30", "31+"))
  )

nrow(nhl)
```

# 1.

**Source:** Hockey-Reference https://www.hockey-reference.com/leagues/NHL_2026_skaters.html 
**Description:** This dataset contains the top 100 player stats for the 2025-2026 NHL season. This includes their age, team, position, scoring stats (G, A, Pts, +/-, PIM), goal related stats (PPG, SHG, GWG), assists (EV, PP, SH), shots (SOG), ice-time, and face-offs. I think it will be interesting to explore this dataset when broken down by each stat, and to see if any of the stats relate to each other. I think it will also be interesting to see this dataset explored by position of the player as well.
**Why this data?:** Counting stats (goals, points, hits) are bounded below by 0, so they should be right-skewed. That makes the data a natural fit for reexpression and resistant methods.

**Continous Variables:** Age, GP (Games Played), G (Goals), A (Assists), PTS (Points), +/- (Plus/Minus), PIM (Penalties in Minutes), EVG (Even Strength Goals), PPG (Power Play Goals), SHG (Shorthanded Goals), GWG (Game-Winning Goals), EV (Even Strength Assists), PP (Power Play Assists), SH (Shorthand Assists), SOG (Shots on Goal), SPCT (Shooting Percentage), TSA (Total Shots Attempted), TOI (Time on Ice, in minutes), ATOI (Avg time on ice, in minutes), FOW (Faceoff Wins), FOL (Faceoff Losses), FO% (Faceoff Percentage), BLK (Blocks), HIT (Hits), TAKE (Takeaways), GIVE (Giveaways)
**Categorical Variables:** Player, Team, Pos (Position)


# 2.

*What does a typical player's point total look like, and who are the outliers?*
```{r}
ggplot(nhl, aes(PTS)) + geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, color = "black", fill = "pink")
aplpack::stem.leaf(nhl$PTS)

# Letter values
lv <- lval(nhl$PTS); lv
fivenum(nhl$PTS)

# Fences and outliers
FL <- lv["H", "lo"]; FU <- lv["H", "hi"]; dF <- FU - FL
fences <- c(FL - 1.5 * dF, FU + 1.5 * dF)
fences
nhl %>% filter(PTS > fences[2] | PTS < fences[1]) %>%
  select(Player, Team, Pos, PTS) %>% arrange(desc(PTS))

# Symmetry checks
lv$mids # increasing midsummaries = right skew
hinkley(nhl$PTS) # d > 0 = right skew
symplot(nhl$PTS) # points above the line = right skew

# Reexpress down the ladder of powers and re-check
ladder <- c(`1` = 1, `0.5` = 0.5, `0` = 0, `-0.5` = -0.5, `-1` = -1)
sapply(ladder, function(p) {
  z <- if (p == 0) log(nhl$PTS) else if (p < 0) -nhl$PTS^p else nhl$PTS^p
  hinkley(z)
})

z <- -nhl$PTS^(-0.5)
aplpack::stem.leaf(round(z, 3))
hinkley(z)
lval(z)$mids
```

A Typical player scores about 70 points (median 70.5), and the middle half of players fall between 62 and 80. The distribution is right-skewed. The mudsummaries climb from 70.5 to 97.5, and Hinley's h is positive (0.19). 4 players are above the upper fence of 107: McDavid (138), Kucherov (130), MacKinnon (127), and Celebrini (115). Reexpressing shrinks the skew (h falls from 0.19 to 0.08 at p = -0.5) but never reaches 0. That is because this is only the top 100 scoreres and the lowest total is 57, so I'd say the data can't be fully symmetrized.

*Do forwards and defensemen differ in scoring? Are the spreads unequal?*
```{r}
# Boxplots ordered by median
ggplot(nhl, aes(reorder(Pos3, PTS, median), PTS)) +
  geom_boxplot() + coord_flip() + xlab("Position")

# Medians and fourth-spreads for each group
nhl %>% group_by(Pos3) %>%
  summarize(n = n(), Median = median(PTS), Spread = IQR(PTS))

# Is spread tied to level?
spread_level_plot(nhl, PTS, Pos3)
# Slope b printed in the title -> suggested power p = 1 - b

# Reexpress using the suggested power 
nhl <- nhl %>% mutate(PTS_new = PTS^(1/3))

ggplot(nhl, aes(reorder(Pos3, PTS_new, median), PTS_new)) +
  geom_boxplot() + coord_flip() + xlab("Position")

nhl %>% group_by(Pos3) %>% summarize(Spread_new = IQR(PTS_new)) %>%
  summarize(ratio_largest_to_smallest = max(Spread_new) / min(Spread_new))
```

Wingers have the highest median (73), then centers (68.5), then defensemen (64.5). Forwards score roughly 4 to 8 points more than defensemen at the median, but the boxes overlap heavily. The spreads are similar (fourth-spreads of about 18.5, 17.8, and 16.5). The spread-level slope of 0.68 suggests a cube root, but it changed the spread ratio only slightly (1.12 to 1.06), so reexpression barely matters. With only 16 defensement, the defense median is less certain.

*Shots vs. goals, and ice time vs. points*
```{r}
# Three summary points
three_pts <- function(df, xvar, yvar) {
  df %>%
    mutate(grp = ntile({{ xvar }}, 3)) %>%
    group_by(grp) %>%
    summarize(x = median({{ xvar }}), y = median({{ yvar }}), .groups = "drop") %>%
    select(x, y) %>% as.data.frame()
}

# transform the summary points and get the half-slope ratio
straightening.work <- function(sp, px, py) {
  sp$tx <- with(sp, (x ^ px - 1) / px)
  sp$ty <- with(sp, (y ^ py - 1) / py)
  sp$slope[1] <- with(sp, diff(ty[1:2]) / diff(tx[1:2]))
  sp$slope[2] <- with(sp, diff(ty[2:3]) / diff(tx[2:3]))
  sp$half.slope.ratio <- with(sp, slope[2] / slope[1])
  sp$slope[3] <- NA
  sp$half.slope.ratio[2:3] <- NA
  row.names(sp) <- c("Left", "Center", "Right")
  sp
}
```

*Shots on goal vs. goals, who over or under performs?*
```{r}
nhl_df <- as.data.frame(nhl)

ggplot(nhl, aes(SOG, G)) + geom_point() + geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE)

sp <- three_pts(nhl_df, SOG, G)
straightening.work(sp, 1, 1)

# Resistant line 
fit_sog <- rline(G ~ SOG, nhl_df, iter = 5)
c(a = fit_sog$a, b = fit_sog$b, xC = fit_sog$xC)
coef(lm(G ~ SOG, nhl))
cor(nhl$SOG, nhl$G)

a  <- as.numeric(unlist(fit_sog$a))
b  <- as.numeric(unlist(fit_sog$b))
xC <- as.numeric(unlist(fit_sog$xC))
c(rline_intercept = a - b * xC, rline_slope = b)
coef(lm(G ~ SOG, nhl))

nhl <- nhl %>%
  mutate(Fit_G   = a + b * (SOG - xC),
         Resid_G = G - Fit_G)

nhl %>% slice_max(Resid_G, n = 5) %>% select(Player, Pos, SOG, G, SPCT, Resid_G)
nhl %>% slice_min(Resid_G, n = 5) %>% select(Player, Pos, SOG, G, SPCT, Resid_G)

ggplot(nhl, aes(SOG, Resid_G, color = Group2)) + geom_point() + geom_hline(yintercept = 0)
```

Shots and goals are moderately strongly related (r = 0.65). The resistant line says each extra shot is worth about 0.13 goals, or one goal per 8 shots. Least squares gives nearly the same slope (0.135). Over performers are Johnston, Caulfield, Geekie, Stamkos, and Kucherov. All shoot about 19-22%, well above what their shot volume predicts. The five biggest under performers are all defensement (Hughes, Seider, Werenski, Sergachev, LaCombe), with shooting percentages of 4-9%. So position explains much of the residual pattern. These are mostly defensemen shooting from distance, not unlucky forwards.

*Does ice time predict points?*
```{r}
nhl_df <- as.data.frame(nhl)

ggplot(nhl, aes(ATOI_min, PTS)) + geom_point() + geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE)

sp2 <- three_pts(nhl_df, ATOI_min, PTS)
straightening.work(sp2, 1, 1)

fit_toi <- rline(PTS ~ ATOI_min, nhl_df, iter = 5)
c(a = fit_toi$a, b = fit_toi$b, xC = fit_toi$xC)
cor(nhl$ATOI_min, nhl$PTS)

a2  <- as.numeric(unlist(fit_toi$a))
b2  <- as.numeric(unlist(fit_toi$b))
xC2 <- as.numeric(unlist(fit_toi$xC))

nhl <- nhl %>%
  mutate(Fit_PTS   = a2 + b2 * (ATOI_min - xC2),
         Resid_PTS = PTS - Fit_PTS)

# Does position explain the leftover pattern? (defensemen have more ice time)
ggplot(nhl, aes(Pos3, Resid_PTS)) + geom_boxplot() + geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "red")
nhl %>% slice_max(Resid_PTS, n = 5) %>% select(Player, Pos, ATOI_min, PTS, Resid_PTS)
nhl %>% slice_min(Resid_PTS, n = 5) %>% select(Player, Pos, ATOI_min, PTS, Resid_PTS)

fwd <- nhl_df %>% filter(Group2 == "Forward")
straightening.work(three_pts(fwd, ATOI_min, PTS), 1, 1)
fit_fwd <- rline(PTS ~ ATOI_min, fwd, iter = 5)
c(slope = as.numeric(unlist(fit_fwd$b)))
cor(fwd$ATOI_min, fwd$PTS)
ggplot(fwd, aes(ATOI_min, PTS)) + geom_point() + geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE)
```

For all players, only weakly (r = 0.27). The curve rises to about 21 minutes and then falls. The drop comes from defensemen, who play roughly 24+ minutes but score less. They have the most negative residuals. Among forwards, the relationship is much stronger (r = 0.66), at roughly 7 extra points per extra minute of ice time. The forward relationship bends upward (half-slope ratio 2.27), because the stars (McDavid, Kucherov, MacKinnon) both play more and score far more.

*How does production change with age?*
```{r}
ggplot(nhl, aes(Age, PTS)) + geom_point() + geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE)

ggplot(nhl, aes(AgeGroup, PTS)) + geom_boxplot() + coord_flip()

nhl %>% group_by(AgeGroup) %>%
  summarize(n = n(), Median = median(PTS), Spread = IQR(PTS))
```

There is no strong age trend. Median points are 69 (less than or equal to age 22), 68 (ages 23-26), 72 (ages 27-30), and 66 (greater than age 31). Production peaks slightly in the late 20s, and the 31+ group has the lowest median and the tightest spread. Each difference is only a few points, small compared to the spread of about 15 points within each age group.

*Do position and age both shape production? is it additive?*
```{r}
# How many players are in each cell? (small cells = shaky medians)
table(nhl$Pos3, nhl$AgeGroup)

tab <- nhl %>%
  group_by(Pos3, AgeGroup) %>% summarize(M = median(PTS), .groups = "drop") %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = AgeGroup, values_from = M) %>%
  as.data.frame() %>% column_to_rownames("Pos3") %>% as.matrix()
tab <- tab[, levels(nhl$AgeGroup)]
tab

# Additive fit
pp <- medpolish(tab)
pp

# Additive fit plot
plot2way(pp$row + pp$overall, pp$col, rownames(tab), colnames(tab))

# Are the effects big compared to the residuals?
round(c(row = range(pp$row), col = range(pp$col), resid = range(pp$residuals)), 2)

# Comparison values
cv <- outer(pp$row, pp$col, "*") / pp$overall
df <- data.frame(cv = as.vector(cv), resid = as.vector(pp$residuals))
ggplot(df, aes(cv, resid)) + geom_point() + geom_hline(yintercept = 0)
```

The common value is about 68 points. Position effects are tiny (center -0.3, defensemen 0, wings +2.6). Age effects are larger: 31+ is -4.9, and ages 27-30 is +1.9. So age matters somewhat more than position here, and neither is big. The residuals go up to +9.8 (31+ centers) and +4.6 (27-30 wings). These are larger than the effects, so the additive model explains little of the table. Cells are small (defensemen only have 2 players in the less than or equal to age 22 and in the 31+ groups), so conclusions are just exploratory. The comparison-value step was unstable, so I'd stay with the additive fit.

*How well does a normal curve describe ice time, and where does it fail?*
```{r}
gaussian_check <- function(x, width = 1) {
  lvx <- lval(x)
  FL <- lvx["H", "lo"]; FU <- lvx["H", "hi"]
  m <- (FU + FL) / 2
  s <- (FU - FL) / 1.349
  bins <- seq(floor(min(x)) - width, ceiling(max(x)) + width, by = width)
  g <- fit.gaussian(x, bins, m, s)
  mids <- (bins[-1] + bins[-length(bins)]) / 2
  print(c(mean_fit = m, sd_fit = s))
  print(data.frame(Mid = mids, d = g$counts, e = round(g$expected, 1),
                   sqrt_d = round(sqrt(g$counts), 2),
                   resid = round(sqrt(g$counts) - sqrt(g$expected), 2)))
  rootogram(g$counts, g$expected)
  rootogram(g$counts, g$expected, type = "deviation")
}

hist(nhl$ATOI_min, breaks = 12)
gaussian_check(nhl$ATOI_min, width = 1)

gaussian_check(nhl$ATOI_min[nhl$Group2 == "Forward"], width = 1)
```

For all players, a normal curve (mean about 19.8, SD about 2.2) fits the middle well. It fails at 24.5 minutes, where there are 7 players but only 2 are expected (that's the defensemen). It also has too few players at 21.5-22.5 minutes and none at 14.5. For forwards only (mean 19.2, SD 1.7), the fit is much better. Nearly every root residual si within +-0.4. So ice time is a mixture of two groups: forwards are close to normal, and defensemen form a second bump at around 24+ minutes. 


# 3. Methods and Interpretation

## a) Single batch

**i) Stemplots** 

The first stemplot breaks at the tens place with 5 leaves per stem. The four largest values are listed on a separate HI line so they don't stretch the display.

```{r}
aplpack::stem.leaf(nhl$PTS, unit = 1, m = 2)
```

The second version uses 10 leaves per stem:

```{r}
aplpack::stem.leaf(nhl$PTS, unit = 1, m = 1)
```

The first stemplot looks better compared to the second one which squeezes most of the data onto three lines. 



**ii) Letter values, the five-number summary, and outliers.**

```{r}
lval(nhl$PTS)
fivenum(nhl$PTS)
FL <- 62; FU <- 80; STEP <- 1.5 * (FU - FL)
c(inner.lo = FL - STEP, inner.hi = FU + STEP,
  outer.lo = FL - 2 * STEP, outer.hi = FU + 2 * STEP)
filter(nhl, PTS > FU + STEP) %>% select(Player, Team, GP, PTS)
```

- **Value and spread:** The median is $M = 70.5$ points and the fourths are 62 and 80. Half of these players scored between 62 and 80 points, so the fourth-spread is $d_F = 18$.

- **Shape:** The mids increase steadily from 70.5 to 71, 74.5, 79, 86, 92.75 and finally 97.5 at the extremes. That is right skew, and it grows stronger toward the tails.

- **Outliers:** The step is 27, so the inner fences are 35 and 107.

- Nobody is beyond the low fences, because the low end of the data is cut off at 57.

**iii) Mean vs. median, and checking symmetry.**

```{r}
c(mean = mean(nhl$PTS), median = median(nhl$PTS))
pts.lv <- lval(nhl$PTS)
pts.lv %>% mutate(LV = 1:nrow(pts.lv)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(LV, mids)) + geom_point() + ggtitle("Midsummaries: Raw PTS")
symplot(nhl$PTS)
hinkley(nhl$PTS)
```

The mean is larger than the median, which is what we expect for right-skewed data. The superstars pull the mean up, but they don't affect the median. Hinkley's $d = 0.19$ is positive. In the symmetry plot, almost all of the points fall above the line $u = v$, and they move farther above it toward the right. That means right skew mostly in the tails.

**iv) Reexpression.** 
```{r reexp-pts}
pts.re <- data.frame(power = c("1 (raw)", "0.5 (roots)", "0 (logs)",
                               "-0.5", "-1"),
  hinkley.d = c(hinkley(nhl$PTS), hinkley(sqrt(nhl$PTS)),
                hinkley(log10(nhl$PTS)), hinkley(-1 / sqrt(nhl$PTS)),
                hinkley(-1 / nhl$PTS)))
pts.re
lval(log10(nhl$PTS))
```

Hinkley's $d$ gets smaller as we go down the ladder. 0.19 for raw data, then 0.15, 0.11, 0.08, and 0.04. Even the reciprocals, p=1, still leaves the batch right-skewed, and the mids of the logs still increase. 

Reexpression does not make this batch symmetric. Reexpression helps most when HI/LO is large, and here HI/LO = 138/57 = 2.4, which is small. 

**iv) Matched transformations.** 
We matched the roots and logs to the raw data at the median, so the three batches can be compared on the same scale.

```{r}
raw <- nhl$PTS
matched.roots <- mtrans(raw, 0.5)
matched.logs <- mtrans(raw, 0)
boxplot(data.frame(raw, matched.roots, matched.logs))
```

In all three boxplots, the middle half is fairly balanced, but the upper whisker is much longer than the lower one and the outliers are all at the high end. The roots and logs pull in the long right tail a little, but they don't remove the skewness. This agrees with Hinkley's $d$.


### Binned data: ice time (ATOI)
With 100 players, we grouped the average ice times ( minutes per game) into bins and compared the bin counts with a Gaussian curve.

#### i) Constructing a histogram

The ice times range from 15.2 to 27.7 minutes, so we used bins of width 1 minute from 14 to 28.

```{r}
bins <- seq(14, 28, 1)
bin.mids <- (bins[-1] + bins[-length(bins)]) / 2
ggplot(nhl, aes(ATOI.min)) +
  geom_histogram(breaks = bins,
                 fill = "white",
                 color = "red") +
  xlab("Average time on ice")
```

Most players have 17-21 minutes a night. The counts drop off at 21-23 minutes, and then there is a second, smaller group at 23-26 minutes.
Large counts vary more than small counts, so it is hard to compare this histogram with a normal curve by eye. We can therefore implement a rootogram.

####ii) A rootogram

```{r}
p <- ggplot(nhl, aes(ATOI.min)) +
     geom_histogram(breaks = bins)
out <- ggplot_build(p)$data[[1]]
select(out, count, x, xmin, xmax)
ggplot(out, aes(x, sqrt(count))) +
  geom_col() + xlab("Average time on ice (minutes)")
```

#### iii) Fitting a Gaussian comparison curve

We matched the Gaussian curve using the fourths:

```{r}
fivenum(nhl$ATOI.min)
```

$$
m = \frac{F_U + F_L}{2} = \frac{21.30 + 18.27}{2} = 19.78, \qquad
s = \frac{F_U - F_L}{1.349} = \frac{21.30 - 18.27}{1.349} = 2.25.
$$

So the matching Gaussian curve is N(19.78, 2.25).

```{r}
s <- fit.gaussian(nhl$ATOI.min, bins, 19.78, 2.25)
options(digits=3)
(df <- data.frame(Mid=bin.mids, d=s$counts, sqrt.d=sqrt(s$counts),
           Prob=s$probs, e=s$expected, sqrt.e=sqrt(s$expected),
           Residual=s$residual))
options(digits=7)
```

```{r}
ggplot(out, aes(x, sqrt(count))) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_line(data = df,
            aes(bin.mids, sqrt.e), color="red") +
  xlab("Average time on ice (minutes)")
```

#### iv) Hanging rootogram

```{r}
library(vcd)
rootogram(s$counts, s$expected)
rootogram(s$counts, s$expected, type="deviation")
```

The bars that fall below the line at 0 are positive residuals (more players than the curve expects), and the bars that stay above the line are negative residuals. 

Double-root residuals:

```{r}
DRR <- sqrt(2 + 4 * s$counts) - sqrt(1 + 4 * s$expected)
data.frame(Mid = bin.mids, d = s$counts, e = round(s$expected, 1),
           DRR = round(DRR, 2))
```

To see who is in each ice-time range, we counted the players by position:

```{r}
table(cut(nhl$ATOI.min, bins), nhl$Group)
```


The normal curve does not fit ice time well, and that shows how NHL lineups are built.

- **There are too many players at 17-19 minutes:** Residuals are between +0.35 and +0.60, and the double-root residual is 1.25. This is where the forwards pile up. Every player in these bins is a forward. Coaches rotate forward lines in short shifts, so most top forwards end up with very similar minutes.
- **There are too few players at 21-23 minutes:** Residuals are between -0.81 and -0.93, and the double-root residuals are between -1.50 and -1.70. This is the gap between the forwards and the defensemen. Only the busiest forwards reach 21 minutes, and only one defenseman plays less than 23.
- **There are too many players at 24-28 minutes:** The 24-25 bin has 7 players when the curve expects 2.0, double-root residual is 2.46, the largest in the table. These are the defensemen. Defense pairs stay on the ice longer, and the top pair on a team can play 25+ minutes a night. Every player above 23 minutes is a defenseman.
- **No one is below 15 minutes**, where the curve expects about 1 player. Players with low ice time rarely score enough to make the top 100 list.

So ice time is really two batches mixed together, forwards and defensemen, and a single bell curve can't describe them both.
